Congenital plexopathy may spontaneously resolve within months; if not, surgery should be considered. B
Protective equipment may be helpful in sports. B

background.definition: The brachial plexus is a complex network of nerves originating from the C5 to T1 nerve roots of the cervical and thoracic spine. The plexus includes trunks, divisions, cords, branches, and then individual nerves. These nerves terminate into the muscles and skin of the arm and shoulder girdle. Brachial plexopathies are a heterogeneous group of conditions that result from injury to one or more portions of the brachial plexus.

list.listitem: Estimated at 0.4 to 4 cases per 1000 live births. Based on 1997, 2000, and 2003 Kids' Inpatient Database data sets, the incidence of neonatal brachial plexus palsy in the US is 1.51 ± 0.02 cases per 1000 live births. In one cohort study at a teaching hospital, brachial plexus injury occurred in 20% of cases of shoulder dystocia.

Incidence is 7.8% following successful McRoberts' maneuver to alleviate shoulder dystocia based on 205 cases at a single institution. Of the subsequent maneuvers used, rotational methods and posterior arm delivery were similarly successful (72% and 63.6%) but the former was associated with less brachial plexus injury (4.4% vs. 21.4%). In another retrospective study of 13,998 singleton deliveries over 10 years in California, 221 (1.6%) had shoulder dystocia and 42 of these (19.0%) had brachial plexus palsy.
Two to 3 cases per 100,000 individuals is the annual incidence for Parsonage-Turner syndrome.
Stingers/burners occur frequently in collision sports; an estimated 65% of football players experience at least 1 such injury during their careers.
Stingers and burners commonly recur; the estimated recurrence rate is 42% to 87%.

Rates of C-5 palsy following cervical spine surgery range from 0% to 30%. About 70% of patients spontaneously recover in about 4 to 5 months. In another study, the incidence of C-5 nerve palsy after cervical spine decompression was 6.7%.

Twenty to 50 pain cases per 1000 patients treated with radiation. Of 352 patients who completed radiation therapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, brachial plexopathy occurred in 14%.
Congenital (Erb's palsy, Erb's palsy plus, Klumpke's palsy)
Traumatic (root avulsion, stinger/burner syndrome, backpack palsy, crutch palsy)
Atraumatic (thoracic outlet syndrome, diabetes-related brachial plexopathy, hereditary brachial plexopathy, brachial neuritis, Parsonage-Turner syndrome)
Iatrogenic (surgically-induced, radiation-induced, associated with brachial plexus block)
Neoplastic (Pancoast's syndrome)

Congenital : may be related to traction-type injury on the brachial plexus from shoulder dystocia during vaginal delivery, though this causation has not been confirmed. In one prospective study, almost half of the injuries followed spontaneous vaginal deliveries with second stages of 30 minutes or less and in another 54% had no known risk factors.

Traumatic : causes include direct compression to the nerve (usually at the supraclavicular fossa or in the axilla), stretching of the nerve, and shearing force resulting in avulsion or axonal disruption. Traction injury or "burners" occur when the shoulder is depressed and neck pressed laterally away from involved side.
Atraumatic : brachial plexopathy includes genetic, metabolic, and possibly infectious etiologies resulting in damage to the nerve and/or surrounding microvasculature.

Iatrogenic : deleterious side effects from radiation on the nerve or injury from compression from positions or direct laceration during surgical procedures results in iatrogenic damage to the brachial plexus.
Neoplastic : direct compression from tumor or tumor invasion directly into the nerve.
Obstetric training may reduce birth injury. B
Evaluate for brachial plexus injury in all cases of shoulder dystocia. B
Data are conflicting about whether planned cesarean delivery vs. planned breech delivery for term singleton breech presentation prevents brachial plexus injury. B

Labor induction for suspected large-for-gestational age infants does not appear to reduce brachial plexus injury. B However, data are conflicting with respect to induction at 41 weeks vs. 42 weeks for low-risk women for prevention of adverse perinatal outcomes. B
Use of cowboy collars and neck rolls have been shown to decrease cervical strain and probably reduces the likelihood of stingers and burners in football players. B

There is no clear evidence to support or refute prophylactic measures to prevent shoulder dystocia and resulting congenital brachial plexus injury. C Authors of a Cochrane review of planned caesarean section for singleton breech presentation at term compared to a vaginal delivery protocol found no difference in brachial plexus injury (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.08-1.47, three studies, 2375 infants [nine events]) or birth trauma.

Obstetric training can reduce injury. In an interrupted time-series study at one large UK hospital, institution of a bi-monthly multi-professional 1-day intrapartum emergencies training course, that included a 30-minute practical session on shoulder dystocia management, improved use of recognized resolution maneuvers and reduced brachial plexus injury at birth from 24/324 (7.4%) in the pre-training period to 6/262 (2.3%) in early training and 7/562 (1.3%) in the late training period.

Planned cesarean delivery vs. planned breech delivery for term singleton breech presentation results in an absolute risk reduction of perinatal mortality, fetal neurologic morbidity, birth trauma, 5-minute Apgar score <7 and neonatal asphyxia of 0.3%, 0.7%, 0.7%, 2.4% and 3.3%, respectively, based on a systematic review of 27 trials and observational studies with a total of 258,953 women.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 trials of labor induction vs. expectant management in 1190 women with suspected large-for-date fetuses or suspected macrosomia found lower mean birthweight and fewer birth fractures or shoulder dystocia with induction; however, there was no difference in brachial plexus injuries which were rare (2 cases in control group). Induction was associated with increased perineal damage and increased use of phototherapy.

In an RCT of 1801 low-risk women in the Netherlands, planned induction at 41 weeks vs. expectant management until 42 weeks resulted in 1.4% difference (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.9% to 0.0%) for risk of adverse perinatal outcomes, including brachial plexus injury; no neonatal deaths occurred and rates were similar for composite adverse maternal outcomes and cesarean section rate.

A similar Swedish RCT of 2760 low-risk women, however, was stopped early because of a significantly higher rate of perinatal mortality in the expectant management group (6 deaths vs. no perinatal deaths in the induction group) although the composite primary perinatal outcome did not differ between the groups (2.4% (33/1381) in the induction group and 2.2% (31/1379) in the expectant management group).

For patients undergoing median sternotomy as a surgical approach, brachial plexus injuries/peripheral neuropathies can be reduced by opening as small a distance as possible, use of a caudally-placed symmetrical retractor, and placing the patient in a “hands up” position. In addition to positioning techniques, another measure that may be useful for secondary prevention is case finding for early recognition of neuropathies to reduce complications.
It may be possible to limit radiation-associated brachial plexopathy in patients with lung cancer by reducing the dose through computer-assisted imaging to better contour the brachial plexus.
Thorough physical examination including complete neuromuscular examination in the context of a proper history is essential. C
Evaluate all traumatic causes of brachial plexus injury with cervical and shoulder x-rays. C
Use EMG as a diagnostic aid for complicated or prolonged courses; MRI is the recommended imaging study for atraumatic plexopathy. C

Consider brachial plexus injury in cancer patients (especially those undergoing radiation) and in collision-sport athletes complaining of burning or tingling unilateral shoulder girdle or arm pain with or without weakness. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Shoulder and arm pain, pain only with resisted rotator cuff motion, distinguishable by MRI
Hand and forearm pain only, distinguishable by EMG
Ulnar sided pain only, distinguishable by EMG

list.listitem: Narakas classification divides infants with brachial plexus injury info 4 groups:
Upper Erb's palsy, extended Erb's palsy, total palsy, and total palsy with Horner's syndrome.
Seddon's classification is used to grade brachial plexopathy in other peripheral nerve injuries.
Grade 1: neuropraxia (focal demyelination or ischemia)
Grade 2: axonotmesis (damage to the axon and sheath with endoneurium, periuneurium and epineurium intact) .
Grade 3: neurotmesis (complete nerve transection), resulting in permanent nerve damage.

Consider brachial plexus injury in cancer patients, especially those undergoing radiation, and in collision athletes complaining of unilateral burning or tingling shoulder girdle or arm pain, with or without motor weakness.

History should clearly delineate the acuity, timing, and comorbidities to categorize the injury as traumatic, congenital, atraumatic, iatrogenic, or neoplastic. For congenital lesions, it must be clearly established that the deficit was present at time of birth. For traumatic lesions, the mechanism of injury is critical. Atraumatic or other idiopathic causes of brachial plexus injury are diagnosed when there is no clear underlying cause, although diabetes and viral infections may be present. For iatrogenic lesions, the injury must be clearly temporally related to surgical or medical treatment. For neoplastic lesions, the symptoms should be related to discovery of a malignancy.

The location and extent of pain, numbness, tingling, and immobility if any is helpful in determining the extent of the lesion. Also ask about the course and duration of symptoms, and alleviating and aggravating factors.

Physical examination should consist of complete head and neck, neurologic, upper extremity musculoskeletal, spine, and cardiopulmonary examinations. Other examinations should be conducted as indicated by history. Particular importance should be placed on muscular strength, sensation, and reflexes in the upper extremities.

In newborns, thumb pain elicited by thumb nail bed compression (testing C-6 sensory fibers) was a useful prognostic indicator in one study. Twenty-six of 30 infants with absent thumb pain sensation had a poor outcome at 6 months of age.

Provocative tests including Spurling's maneuver (high specificity, low sensitivity) for cervical nerve compression; Adson's test, Wright's test, and Roos test in the upper extremity should be performed as indicated.
If patient has evidence of Horner's syndrome, this is concerning for complete lower plexus injury.
Cervical spine and shoulder x-rays are required for any traumatic injury to rule out fracture or dislocation.

EMG/NCS are helpful for distinguishing between type of brachial plexopathies as well as differentiating brachial plexopathy from other central and peripheral nerve injuries. In one case series of neonatal brachial plexus palsy, EMG at 1 month was predictive of severe cases of flexion paralysis at 3 months. Findings were less useful with EMG performed at 3 months of age.
A pressure-specified sensory device was more sensitive than EMG in one study and consistently identified injuries that were not detected by needle EMG tests.

MRI without contrast is the recommended initial study by the American College of Radiology (ACR) for patients with atraumatic neurogenic shoulder pain. MRI of shoulder and brachial plexus without and with contrast may identify constrictions, impingement or injury to the brachial plexus, and also will rule out other musculoskeletal causes of shoulder and arm pain.

For patients with new or increasing nontraumatic cervical radiculopathy, MRI of the neck without contrast is deemed usually appropriate by ACR to rule out central causes of shoulder and arm pain such as cervical disk syndrome causing nerve root impingement. In one study, the overall positive likelihood ratio (LR) for MRI for adult brachial plexopathy was 9.4, negative LR was 0.21, and accuracy was 0.88.
For patients with traumatic neurogenic shoulder pain and negative initial radiographs, ACR recommends MRI without contrast as the next imaging study; Tc-99m bone scan shoulder may be appropriate.

For patients with traumatic nerve root avulsions, MRI appears to offer modest diagnostic accuracy. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies with 275 adults with traumatic brachial plexus injuries, most from motorcycle collisions, found at least one root avulsion in 72%. MRI had a mean sensitivity for root avulsion of 93% (95% CI, 77%-98%) and mean specificity of 72% (95% CI, 42%-90%) using the nerve root as the unit of analysis.

For patients with atraumatic neurogenic shoulder pain, ACR notes that shoulder ultrasound may be appropriate as this modality can identify paralabral cysts that extend to the spinoglenoid notch, suprascapular notch, and quadrilateral space as well as associated loss of muscle bulk. Authors of a review of ultrasound for atraumatic brachial plexopathies state that US is particularly good for assessing nerve sheath tumors, perineural fibrosis, metastases, some inflammatory neuropathies, neuralgic amyotrophy, and posttraumatic sequalae.

CT of thje cervical spine provides increased sensitivity for detection of fracture or, when used in combination with myelogram, may also detect nerve root injury. MRI is preferred for soft tissue problems. ACR notes that cervical spine CT is usually appropriate (as is radiography) in cases with prior cervical spine surgery or chronic neck pain with or without radiculopathy, and may be appropriate for cases of new or increasing nontraumatic cervical radiculopathy.

Symptoms include unilateral pain, described as a burning or tingling in the arm and shoulder. Symptoms may occur suddenly due to trauma or may start insidiously. Symptoms may be purely sensory but commonly there is associated motor weakness.
Imaging of the neck and shoulder are required for any traumatic cause. If no fracture is noted on x-ray and symptoms resolve quickly after a traumatic cause, no further workup or treatment is needed.
For all other causes, nerve conduction studies are helpful in arriving at the diagnosis.
Physical therapy is the mainstay of treatment for most types of brachial plexopathy. B
Anti-inflammatory medication may be helpful in certain atraumatic cases. C
Surgical intervention should be considered for severe traumatic injury as well as iatrogenic, congenital lesions not improving at 3 months, and neoplastic causes. B
Anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs, oral glucocorticosteroids) are advocated in many cases; however, benefit is unclear.
Antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and narcotics may have a role in treatment for chronic long-term pain and as treatment for postoperative pain following surgery for brachial plexus injury.
No conclusive evidence of shows a benefit of surgery over conservative measures for congenital causes.

Surgical intervention should be considered in congenital cases that do not spontaneously resolve within 3 months. In one case series of nerve transfers, most of the 31 children with neonatal brachial plexus palsy achieved functional recovery of elbow flexion with about 1 in 5 achieving functional supination.

Surgical intervention is appropriate if the brachial plexus injury involves an avulsion of the plexus from a traumatic cause or if atraumatic causes are found that restrict the plexus and are surgically amenable.

In a systematic review of 31 studies of patients with complete traumatic upper brachial plexus injuries of C5-C6, the pooled data favored use of dual nerve transfer over traditional nerve grafting for restoration of shoulder and elbow function. Use of contralateral C7 nerve root transfers patients with brachial plexus root avulsion injuries is controversial with case series showing both good and poor results.

In a more recent meta-analysis of 29 studies with 341 patients with C5 to C6 lesions, there were no differences in numbers reaching grade 3 or higher elbow flexion between single and double fascicular nerve transfers (95.6% vs. 97.5%, respectively), but more patients in the double-transfer group achieved grade 4 or more if preoperative delay was 6 months or less (84 of 101 [83%] vs. 49 of 51 [96%] in the double transfer group).

Authors of a systematic review comparing nerve transfer with nerve repair for the treatment of adult upper brachial plexus injury found no differences between methods in muscle strength scores for shoulder abduction. For elbow flexion recovery, nerve transfer was somewhat more effective than nerve repair.

Functional muscle transfer was superior to late (12 months or more) nerve reconstruction in restoring elbow flexion and strength in adult patients with traumatic brachial plexus palsy based on a systematic review of 33 studies with 103 total patients. Grade M3 or greater strength was observed in 70% of patients undergoing muscle transfer vs. 37% with reconstruction.
In a small case series of 40 patients following nerve injury, there were no differences in strength of elbow flexion between the groups treated with single or double muscle reinnervation.

The incidence of donor-site morbidity after contralateral C7 transfer is relatively high, based on a systematic review; severe and long-term defects occurred occasionally. The authors concluded that contralateral C7 transfer should only be considered when other donor nerves are not available.
Other surgically amenable causes of brachial plexus injury include thoracic outlet syndrome and Pancoast's syndrome.
Cannibis extract demonstrates improved sleep in patients suffering from brachial plexus avulsion. Cannabis was not effective in one clinical trial.
Physical therapy (PT) is the mainstay of treatment for all type of brachial plexopathies.
Even cases of congenital brachial plexopathy may benefit from PT involving passive manual medicine techniques.

In a small RCT of 16 patients, electrical stimulation compared with conventional physiotherapy resulted in significantly improved shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, wrist extension, and arm circumference at 6 weeks in infants with Erb's palsy. It is not clear whether evaluators were blinded to the treatment. In another small study of 42 children aged 3 to 5 years with obstetric brachial plexus injury, neuromuscular electrical stimulation during weight-bearing exercises plus a selected program improved shoulder function over the selected program only, although both groups improved following treatment.
Avoid use of a sling. This may potentially cause a fixed and internally rotated shoulder.
Acupuncture, hypnosis, and biofeedback may have a role in improving chronic neuropathic pain.
Hyperbaric oxygen is not effective.

Botulinum toxin A treatment has also been used for children with obstetric brachial plexus injury, but supporting evidence is limited. Safety of these injections in infants appears similar to that of older children, with no reports of severe adverse effects and rates of 5% to 25% for mild to moderate adverse events, based on a systematic review of 473 infants of whom 112 had obstetric brachial plexus palsy.
Consultation with physiatrist, neurologist, or neurosurgeon is recommended for complicated lesions, catastrophic injury, neoplastic causes, or in idiopathic cases.

In a series of 56 children, one-third resolved completely with conservative therapy within 3 weeks; one-third resolved completely with conservative therapy by 16 months; and one-third did not resolve completely. B In another case-control study with 168 children with brachial plexus birth palsy, 86% of children with C5-C6 and 38% of children with C5-C6-C7 injuries had complete recovery; children with global injuries (C5-Th1) always had permanent disability.

In a meta-analysis of 11 studies (only one of highest quality) of neonatal brachial plexus palsy, 65% of the Narakas I and II groups had complete recovery at 6 months of age and 14% of the Narakas III and IV groups had recovery; most of the recovery was seen by 3 months.
Among patients with persistent shoulder weakness following neonatal brachial plexus palsy, a majority had glenohumeral abduction deformities, with contractures as severe as 65°.

If surgical repair is required for congenital injury, 1 series found that 89% of patients have a good or excellent motor result after 2 years, whereas another found that 63% were satisfied with the outcome at 5 years. B
Most traumatic causes occur during sports and resolve spontaneously, but burners and stingers are commonly recurrent. B

Congenital brachial plexopathies should be considered in all children with shoulder dystocia. Fetal macrosomia may predispose to shoulder dystocia. Etiology has been attributed to iatrogenic lateral traction on the fetal head.
As infants cannot complain of symptoms such as burning and tingling, it is unknown how often transient sensory neurologic symptoms occur.
At least 5 different patterns of congenital nerve injury to the brachial plexus have been described.
C5 to C6 injury, known as Erb's palsy, accounts for 50% of cases. Weakness involves deltoid and infraspinatus muscles resulting in an adducted and internally rotated arm with extended forearm.
C5 through C7 injury is the classic Erb's palsy (Erb's palsy plus) resulting in the "waiter's tip position."
C5 to T1 injuries result in total arm paralysis.
C8 to T1 injuries are known as Klumpke's palsy and result in isolated hand paralysis.
Most cases are self-limited and spontaneously resolve within several months without treatment. Approximately 10% to 25% of patients have residual deficits; surgery may be considered in these cases.

In one follow-up study of 319 children with brachial plexus birth palsy, nearly half (48%) developed elbow flexion contracture at a median age of 5 years. The magnitude of the contracture increased by 4.4% per year before treatment, and was reduced by casting (although contractures increased again at the same rate of 4.4% per year afterwards). Splinting reduced the rate of increase to <0.1% per year.
